lines.text: In medieval England, selling a light loaf of bread could ruin your whole life.
In 1266, the king passed a law fixing exactly how much bread a penny had to buy.
Inspectors went from shop to shop with scales, weighing every single loaf.
Come up short, and you could be fined, whipped, or locked in the pillory while the whole town threw garbage at you.
The problem? Dough shrinks in the oven, and no baker could make every loaf perfect.
So bakers started throwing in one extra loaf with every twelve.
And that's why thirteen is still called a baker's dozen.
